activities.anchor: are writing menus from an empty pantry
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the day-one sketcher
activities.name: fdrMenuPredict

config.q: A designer skips research and starts sketching on day one. What is the most likely result?
choices: A collection with a strong point of view — instinct is enough
Generic garments that say nothing in particular — a menu written from an empty pantry
The same outcome, just arrived at faster
config.why: Nobody opens a restaurant by writing the menu first: they taste, shop and find what the season offers — the menu is the last, shortest step. Research is how a designer finds the something worth saying.

activities.anchor: material you generated or experienced yourself
activities.caption: file each find: made by you, or made by someone else
activities.name: fdrPrimaryBuckets

config.prompt: Primary or secondary — file each piece of research material:
buckets: primary — you made or experienced it

items.label: photographs you took at a vintage market
a scarf you unravelled to see how it was knitted

config.why: Both are legitimate — but the items only you could have collected are what make the book yours rather than a shared board.

activities.caption: the argument and its contract — drag between them
activities.name: fdrBookCompare

config.prompt: Two surfaces, two jobs — drag the divider:

before.label: the research book
before.text: Tens of pages, edited ruthlessly — each spread composed deliberately, like a magazine editor composes a story, so a stranger could follow the argument.

after.label: the moodboard
after.text: One compressed surface: palette, key textures, silhouette references and atmosphere words — the whole mood absorbed in a single glance.

config.why: The board is the collection's contract with itself: when a sketch later drifts off-mood, the board is what pulls it back.

activities.caption: true or false — the volume fallacy
activities.name: fdrVolumeJudge

statements.s: Thirty images that all respond to each other beat three hundred collected indiscriminately.
statements.why: Depth of engagement — drawing over a photograph, testing a colour, taking a garment apart — is what is judged, not volume of clippings.

statements.s: A degree-level research book for one project typically runs hundreds of pages.
statements.why: Tens of pages, not hundreds — editing ruthlessly is the skill.

statements.s: Annotation externalises judgement, which is the thing being graded.
statements.why: A note like 'this drape flattens the silhouette; try the crisper poplin' shows decision-making.

statements.s: Pasting images alone is a standard research verb.
statements.why: Photocollage, traced silhouettes, fabric-manipulation samples and colour chips pulled from photographs are the verbs — pasting alone is not.

activities.anchor: Judges and tutors read the distance between reference and outcome
activities.caption: put the design on the distance dial
activities.name: fdrDistancePlace

config.prompt: Reference and outcome: where should a strong design land on the distance dial?
config.why: Too close is pastiche, too far is incoherence — the sweet spot in between is where a designer's handwriting appears.

activities.anchor: Research is where this coherence is born
activities.caption: three checks that make a line-up an ensemble
activities.name: fdrChecksOrder

config.prompt: Born in research — put the line-up checks in working order:
items: The mood board fixes the palette
The fabric board fixes the materials
Every look is checked against both
config.why: Collections are designed from the inside out: the boards set the constraints first, and only then does each look — statement, core or commercial — have to answer to them.

activities.anchor: The same sketch executed in three fabrics is three different garments
activities.caption: pair each cloth with what it wants to become
activities.name: fdrFabricMatch

config.prompt: Three fabrics, one sketch, three garments — pair each cloth with its behaviour:

pairs.right: the bias cut — cloth falls diagonally across the grain and drapes like poured water
builds architecture — holds a sculpted shoulder or a bell-shaped skirt on its own
shapes itself — stretches over the body without a single dart

config.why: Drape-first is the professional habit: pin cloth on the stand early, let its behaviour edit the drawing, and treat the fabric board as half the collection's identity.

activities.caption: one century, three returns — set the chronology
activities.name: fdrHistoryOrder

config.prompt: The archive cycles — put these silhouettes in chronological order:
items: 1920s — the waist drops and the skirt shortens to liberate movement
1947 — Dior's New Look cinches the waist and pours out the skirt after rationing
1990s — the minimalists strip back to the slip dress and the bias cut
config.why: The designer who knows the century sees revivals, reactions and remixes with named sources — history is the vocabulary the present speaks with an accent.
